papers.title: Power, Performance, and Area of HPC-Based Malware Detectors: An FPGA and Open-PDK ASIC Study
authors: Alireza Abolhasani Zeraatkar, Parnian Shabani Kamran, Parsa Mirfasihi, Saleh Khalaj Monfared, Hussain Al-Asaad
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2610.12795v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Hardware malware detectors (HMDs) classify programs as benign or malicious based on hardware performance counter (HPC) data. Previous studies have shown that ensemble classifiers outperform other classifiers on detection metrics. However, the area, power, and timing costs of HMDs remain open questions. We address these questions across a comprehensive design space comprising multiple classifier families, variable HPC sets, and ensemble learning methods. We designed a pipeline to reconstruct selected trained models, generate synthesizable register-transfer-level (RTL) implementations, validate each design against a bit-accurate golden model, and evaluate the implementations. papers.title: Breaking Memory Bottlenecks in Quantum Control Systems for More Precise Experiments and Higher Throughput Computing
authors: Yicheng Guang, Neel Vora, Yilun Xu, Yueqi Chen, Gang Huang
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2608.06318v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As quantum computing matures, there is an increasing need for deeper and longer experiments to characterize quantum devices precisely and higher circuit throughput to validate more domain applications. However, this need is hindered by a memory bottleneck at the quantum control system layer, arising from the limited capacity of on-chip block random-access memory (BRAM) and the non-deterministic latency of dynamic random-access memory (DRAM). To break this bottleneck, we present Ant-Q, a memory hierarchy design for the QubiC 2.0 control system that integrates DRAM with BRAM to support pipelined quantum circuit execution while keeping inter-circuit timing deterministic whenever each circuit outlasts the refill of the next. papers.title: Anechoic: Onsager-Corrected Parallel Annealing for Sub-0.1 ms Dense Max-Cut on an FPGA
authors: Seungki Hong, Kyeongwon Jeong, Taekwang Jang
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2610.13368v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ising machines solve combinatorial optimization problems by annealing a network of spins. On dense problems, the least expensive hardware step updates all spins at once: stochastic cellular automata (SCA) decide every spin in parallel and read couplings only for the spins that flip. Such synchronous updates create an echo: the previous state of each spin returns to it through its neighbors. On K2000, a Max-Cut benchmark on a 2,000-node complete graph, two-thirds of all flips undo the same spin's flip one step earlier. This paper presents Anechoic, an FPGA Ising machine that subtracts this echo from every decision.
